q: What is maximum likelihood estimation?
short: Choosing the parameters that make the observed data most probable: θ̂ = argmax Π f(xᵢ|θ), usually via the log-likelihood.
detail: Recipe: write LL(θ), differentiate, solve (or use gradient ascent). Assumes IID data.
example: Coin with 7 heads in 10 tosses: θ̂ = 0.7.
follow: Why maximise the log instead of the likelihood?
mistakes: Forgetting the IID assumption.

q: MLE vs MAP?
short: MLE maximises P(data|θ); MAP maximises P(data|θ)P(θ), adding a prior.
detail: MAP = MLE with a uniform prior; MAP ≈ MLE with lots of data. Log-prior acts as a regulariser.
example: Coin 3/3 heads: MLE 1.0, MAP with Beta(5,5) ≈ 0.64.
mistakes: Calling MAP a full Bayesian method.

q: State Bayes' theorem and name its parts.
short: P(h|D) = P(D|h)P(h)/P(D): posterior = likelihood × prior / evidence.
detail: P(D) normalises; for argmax over h it can be dropped.
follow: Why is P(D) hard to compute in general?
mistakes: Mixing up P(D|h) and P(h|D).

q: Why is least squares justified probabilistically?
short: If y = θᵀx + ε with ε ~ N(0, σ²), the log-likelihood is −Σ(y − θᵀx)²/2σ² + constant, so MLE = least squares.
detail: Laplace noise gives absolute error instead; heteroscedastic noise gives weighted least squares.
mistakes: Saying least squares needs no assumptions to be optimal.

q: What is the Naïve Bayes assumption?
short: Features are conditionally independent given the class: P(x₁..xₙ|y) = Π P(xᵢ|y).
detail: Reduces parameters from exponential to linear in n; usually false but often works for classification.
mistakes: Saying features must be independent overall.

q: How is a Naïve Bayes classifier trained on categorical data?
short: By counting: π_k = #class/N and θ_ijk = #(value ∧ class)/#class, optionally smoothed.
detail: One pass over the data; no optimisation.
follow: How is a new example classified?
mistakes: Normalising by the total dataset size instead of class size.

q: What is Laplace smoothing and why is it needed?
short: Add 1 to every count and the number of possible values d to the denominator: (N_ic + 1)/(N_c + d), so no probability is zero.
detail: One zero factor would make the whole product zero. The m-estimate generalises it with a prior p and weight m.
mistakes: Adding 1 to the numerator only.

q: How does Gaussian Naïve Bayes handle numeric features?
short: It models each feature in each class as a normal distribution, estimating μ and σ², and uses the density at x as P(xᵢ|y).
detail: Densities can exceed 1; use log-densities to avoid underflow.
follow: What if a feature is skewed?
mistakes: Using one variance for all classes without saying so.

q: Generative vs discriminative models?
short: Generative models learn P(x, y) = P(y)P(x|y) (Naïve Bayes); discriminative models learn P(y|x) directly (logistic regression).
detail: Generative can sample data and handle missing features; discriminative often more accurate with lots of data.
follow: What does Gaussian NB imply for P(y|x)?
mistakes: Saying generative models can't classify.

q: Why can we drop P(x) when classifying with Bayes' rule?
short: It is the same for every class, so argmax_y P(x|y)P(y)/P(x) = argmax_y P(x|y)P(y).
detail: You need it only to report normalised probabilities.
mistakes: Reporting unnormalised scores as probabilities.

q: Derive the MLE for a Bernoulli parameter p.
short: LL = Σ[xᵢ log p + (1 − xᵢ) log(1 − p)]; dLL/dp = k/p − (n − k)/(1 − p) = 0 ⇒ p̂ = k/n.
detail: k successes in n trials. MAP with Beta(a, b): (k + a − 1)/(n + a + b − 2).
mistakes: Dropping the (1 − xᵢ) term.

q: Derive the gradient of the logistic regression log-likelihood.
short: ∂LL/∂θⱼ = Σ(yᵢ − σ(θᵀxᵢ))xᵢⱼ, using σ' = σ(1 − σ).
detail: No closed form; gradient ascent θ := θ + α∇LL. Equivalent to minimising cross-entropy.
mistakes: Forgetting the chain rule factor x.

q: Solve the session's discrete MLE problem.
short: Counts 0:2, 1:3, 2:3, 3:2 give LL = 5 log θ + 5 log(1 − θ) + const; dLL/dθ = 5/θ − 5/(1 − θ) = 0 ⇒ θ̂ = 0.5.
follow: What if all observations were 0 or 1?
mistakes: Treating the constants 2/3 as depending on θ.

q: Show that a Gaussian prior on weights gives ridge regression.
short: MAP: maximise LL + log P(θ) with θ ~ N(0, τ²I): −Σ(y − θᵀx)²/2σ² − ‖θ‖²/2τ², i.e. minimise SSE + λ‖θ‖² with λ = σ²/τ².
detail: Laplace prior gives lasso.
example: Regularisation as prior belief that weights are small.
follow: What λ for a very wide prior?
mistakes: Thinking regularisation has no probabilistic meaning.

q: Bayes optimal classifier vs MAP hypothesis: give an example where they disagree.
short: Posteriors 0.4, 0.3, 0.3; h1 says +, h2 and h3 say −. MAP hypothesis h1 predicts +; Bayes optimal sums 0.4 for + and 0.6 for − ⇒ −.
detail: Bayes optimal is the best possible on average given H and the prior, but it may not correspond to any single h in H.
mistakes: Assuming the best hypothesis always gives the best prediction.

q: What does the Gibbs algorithm guarantee?
short: Sampling one hypothesis from the posterior gives expected error ≤ 2× the Bayes optimal error (under the right prior).
detail: Cheap: no sum over H.
follow: When might the bound not hold?
mistakes: Thinking Gibbs is always as good as Bayes optimal.

q: Classify 'a very close game' with Laplace-smoothed multinomial NB.
detail: |V| = 14, Sports words = 11, Not = 9.
follow: What if we used Bernoulli NB?
mistakes: Using document counts instead of word counts in the denominator.

q: Why does Naïve Bayes produce over-confident probabilities?
short: Correlated features are counted as independent evidence, so their effects multiply and push posteriors toward 0 or 1.
detail: Rankings may still be good; calibrate (Platt or isotonic) when probabilities matter.
example: Duplicate a feature: its evidence doubles.
mistakes: Trusting NB probabilities as is.

q: Your text NB classifier underflows to zero on long documents. Fix?
short: Sum log-probabilities: log π + Σ log θ; compare log-scores; use log-sum-exp to normalise.
detail: Never multiply hundreds of small probabilities in floating point.
mistakes: Rescaling probabilities by hand.

q: Multinomial vs Bernoulli Naïve Bayes for text?
short: Multinomial uses word counts (frequency matters); Bernoulli uses presence/absence of every vocabulary word, including absent ones.
detail: Multinomial usually better for longer documents; Bernoulli can do well on short texts.
follow: How does each treat a word that appears 5 times?
mistakes: Using Bernoulli NB but ignoring absent words.

q: Show that Gaussian NB with shared variances gives a logistic posterior.
short: log[P(y=1|x)/P(y=0|x)] = log π/(1 − π) + Σ[(μᵢ₁ − μᵢ₀)xᵢ/σᵢ² + (μᵢ₀² − μᵢ₁²)/2σᵢ²], linear in x ⇒ P(y=1|x) = σ(w₀ + wᵀx).
detail: With class-specific variances the log-odds become quadratic (QDA-like).
follow: When do LR and GNB differ?
mistakes: Claiming GNB and LR always give the same weights.

q: Is the MLE always a good estimator?
short: It is consistent and asymptotically efficient under regularity conditions, but can be biased (Gaussian variance with 1/n) and overfit with little data (p̂ = 1 for 3/3 heads).
detail: MAP/Bayesian priors or regularisation help in small samples.
mistakes: Assuming unbiasedness.

q: How does conjugacy simplify Bayesian updating?
short: A conjugate prior gives a posterior in the same family: Beta-Bernoulli, Dirichlet-multinomial, Normal-Normal. Updating just adds counts.
detail: Laplace smoothing = posterior mean under a uniform Dirichlet(1) prior.
follow: What is the Dirichlet prior in text NB?
mistakes: Thinking Laplace smoothing is ad hoc only.

q: A feature value appears in test data but never in training for any class. What happens in NB?
short: With Laplace smoothing all classes get the same factor 1/(N_c + d) (differing only via N_c); without smoothing every class scores 0.
detail: Common choice: ignore unseen words in text (as the lab does) or reserve an 'unknown' token.
mistakes: Letting all scores become 0 and predicting arbitrarily.

q: What is the posterior predictive distribution and how is it related to the Bayes optimal classifier?
short: p(y|x, D) = ∫ p(y|x, θ)p(θ|D)dθ: average predictions over the posterior. The Bayes optimal classifier is its discrete-hypothesis version.
detail: Bayesian neural networks, MC dropout and ensembles approximate it.
follow: How does MC dropout approximate it?
mistakes: Using only the MAP θ and calling it Bayesian.

q: Gaussian NB on a feature with variance ≈ 0 in one class. Problem?
short: The density becomes a spike: near-infinite at the mean and ≈ 0 elsewhere, so one feature decides everything (as in the humidity example with sd 1.15).
detail: Add variance smoothing (sklearn var_smoothing), use more data, or transform the feature.
mistakes: Ignoring tiny variances.

q: What does m in the m-estimate represent?
short: The equivalent sample size: how many 'virtual' examples drawn from prior p are added: (N_ic + mp)/(N_c + m).
detail: m = d and p = 1/d recovers Laplace smoothing.
mistakes: Thinking m is the number of classes.

q: When would you choose Naïve Bayes over logistic regression in production?
short: Very small training sets, very high-dimensional sparse features, need for incremental/online updates by counting, or many classes with fast training.
detail: LR wins with more data and correlated features; NB converges faster (Ng & Jordan).
example: Real-time ticket routing with daily retraining.
mistakes: Choosing by habit.

q: Why does the Laplace-noise MLE lead to MAE and what does it estimate?
short: The Laplace log-likelihood is −Σ|y − μ|/θ + const, so MLE minimises absolute error, whose minimiser is the conditional median.
detail: Robust to outliers; non-differentiable at 0 (use LP or subgradients).
mistakes: Saying MAE estimates the mean.

q: How would you handle a mix of categorical, count and continuous features in NB?
short: Use the appropriate class-conditional model per feature (categorical counts, multinomial/Poisson, Gaussian or KDE) and multiply (sum logs).
detail: sklearn needs separate models combined by summing log-probabilities and subtracting the repeated log-prior.
follow: How do you avoid counting the prior twice?
mistakes: Binning continuous features without thinking.
